title: Scientists Picked the Day Humanity Ends: November 13, 2026
description: November 4, 1960: the journal Science published 'Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026'. Heinz von Foerster's population curve raced to infinity on that date, and for about 30 years it beat most forecasts. Here's what broke it.

facts.claim: The paper 'Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026' appeared in Science on November 4, 1960
Authors were Heinz von Foerster (physicist, cybernetics pioneer) and his students Patricia M. Mora and Lawrence W. Amiot
They used 24 estimates of world population spanning about 2,000 years and projected population would approach infinity on November 13, 2026
Hyperbolic growth: each doubling takes less time than the last, so the line reaches a vertical wall at a specific date; faster than exponential
Reasoning that more people bring more cooperation and innovation, allowing even faster growth
The paper said descendants would not starve but would be 'squeezed to death'
It drew wide public attention (Time, New York Times); mathematicians and demographers attacked it in letters, calling it absurd
Its projections beat most professional forecasts for about 30 years (1970s-1980s); around 1993 the global population began falling behind the forecasts
Today the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate
Global population now around 8.3 billion; UN projects a peak around 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s
He was at one point in his life a stage magician / known for his interest in magic
No scientific reason to treat November 13, 2026 as a real doomsday; it is a mathematical singularity of the model

careful: Real people (Heinz von Foerster and his two students) are shown only as faceless mannequins, with public facts only. The students are not named in the narration. The video makes clear this was a model that failed, not a real doomsday prediction. The birthday is stated only as a fact; there is no claim that he picked the date because of it. Policy angles are left out on purpose: the paper's birth-rate recommendation, the court and pesticide citations, and the causes of falling birth rates. 'Squeezed to death' is a paraphrase of the paper's warning, and no gore is shown.

trend.why_now: The 1960 paper 'Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026' is going around again because that date is almost here. Fact-check and explainer articles ran from Oct 1 to Oct 31, and interest should peak just before Nov 13, which is six days after this episode goes out.
trend.pattern: Follows the viral 'scientists once calculated the date of doomsday and it's next month' angle. The hook reveals the date, then sets up the real paper, then turns on the creepy fact that it was accurate for 30 years, then returns things to normal. The title states the date, countdown style, so it still works before and after Friday.
